lesson.intro:
Almost everything else in this course is about other road users: who goes first, how fast, where you may stop. This module is about the one and a half tonnes of metal you are sitting in. It is the *Zusatzstoff*, the class-B-specific extra material, and it quietly catches people out, because you cannot work it out by watching traffic. The examiner wants proof that you can spot a worn tyre, set a head restraint, strap down a flat-pack wardrobe and tow a friend's dead Golf off the A100 without making everything worse.

The good news: it is one idea wearing several costumes. **Before you turn the key, the vehicle, the load and the passengers are your responsibility**, not the garage's, not the mate who lent you the trailer. Learn the handful of numbers in here (1.6 mm, 150 cm, 750 kg, 1.5 m, 30 × 30 cm) and the rest is common sense with a paragraph number attached.

sections.heading: Tyres: four postcards of rubber
sections.body:
Your car touches the road on four contact patches roughly the size of a postcard. Steering, braking, aquaplaning, that greasy tram rail on Bergmannstraße in October drizzle. All of it happens there. Which is why the exam asks far more about tyres than about engines.

**Tread depth (Profiltiefe).** The legal minimum is **1.6 mm** in the main tread grooves, right around the circumference. Below that it is a 60 € fine plus a point in Flensburg, and your insurer will take a keen interest after a crash. But legal is not the same as safe: wet grip collapses long before you reach the limit, so tyre testers advise replacing summer tyres at about **3 mm** and winter tyres at about **4 mm**. Free gauge in your pocket: the gold rim of a 1-euro coin is 3 mm wide, the silver rim of a 2-euro coin is 4 mm. Push the coin into the groove. If the rim disappears, you still have that much tread.

**Winter tyres.** Germany has no calendar rule; the duty is *situational*. In black ice, packed snow, slush, ice or frost slipperiness (*Glatteis, Schneeglätte, Schneematsch, Eisglätte, Reifglätte*) you may only drive if **all** wheels, not just the driven ones, wear proper winter tyres. And since **1 October 2024** "proper" means the **Alpine symbol** (*Alpine-Symbol*: a three-peaked mountain with a snowflake). The old **M+S** marking on its own is no longer enough; the transitional period for those tyres ran out on 30 September 2024. The dealer slogan *"von O bis O"*, Oktober bis Ostern, is a sensible habit, not a law.

**Pressure (Reifendruck).** Check it regularly, roughly every two weeks and before a long trip, ideally on cold tyres, using the car maker's figures: the sticker in the fuel filler flap, on the driver's door pillar, or in the manual. Under-inflation is not "softer and safer": rolling resistance rises (more fuel), the tyre flexes and overheats (risk of failure at speed), and the shoulders wear away and the steering goes vague. Cars first registered from November 2014 have tyre-pressure monitoring (*Reifendruckkontrollsystem*), but it warns late and does not replace a gauge.

**Age.** Rubber hardens even when the car just stands in the courtyard. The four-digit **DOT** number on the sidewall gives week and year of manufacture, so "0824" means week 8 of 2024. There is no legal maximum age for car tyres, but plan on replacing them after roughly six to eight years even if tread is left.

callout.text: M+S without the Alpine symbol has been legally useless in winter since 1 October 2024. Driving on it in wintry conditions: 60 € and a point, rising to 80 € if you obstruct others and 100 € if you endanger them.

sections.heading: Lights, checks and warning lamps
sections.body:
Learn the family first: side/parking lights (*Standlicht, Begrenzungsleuchten*), dipped beam (*Abblendlicht*), main beam (*Fernlicht*), daytime running lights (*Tagfahrlicht*), front fog lights (*Nebelscheinwerfer*), rear fog light (*Nebelschlussleuchte*), brake lights (*Bremsleuchten*), indicators (*Fahrtrichtungsanzeiger*), hazard warning lights (*Warnblinkanlage*), reversing light (*Rückfahrscheinwerfer*), number-plate light, and the red rear reflectors.

**All of it has to work, in daylight too.** A blown bulb is already a defect, not a job for next weekend, and "the other headlight still works" is no defence. So walk round the car now and then with the lights on. Indicators and brake lights are the ones you cannot see from the driver's seat: either ask someone to stand behind the car, or reverse gently towards a shop window or garage door and watch the reflection while you press the pedal.

**Which light when.** At dusk, in darkness, and whenever visibility demands it, you use dipped beam. Parking lights are for a parked car, never for driving. Daytime running lights are no substitute after dark, because on most cars they light only the front, so your tail lights stay dark and you become invisible from behind. Front fog lights are for genuinely poor visibility from fog, snowfall or rain. The **rear fog light is stricter: fog only, and only when visibility drops below 50 m**, at which point you must not exceed 50 km/h anyway. Switch it off as the fog lifts; it dazzles the car behind and swamps your brake lights.

**Warning lamps.** Red means *now*, yellow means *soon*:

- **Oil pressure (red)**: stop as soon as you safely can and switch the engine off. A few minutes without oil pressure can wreck an engine.
- **Brake warning (red)**: low brake fluid or a fault in the system. Do not drive on. Get it checked.
- **Coolant temperature (red)**: the engine is overheating. Stop, let it cool, and never open a hot expansion tank.
- **Battery/charge (red)**: the alternator is not charging; everything electrical is living off the battery.

And the diary item: a car goes for its roadworthiness test (*Hauptuntersuchung*, HU, which everybody calls "TÜV") **three years** after first registration, then every **two years**.

callout.text: Rear fog light: fog only, visibility under 50 m only, and then 50 km/h maximum. It is the most misused switch in Germany.

sections.heading: Set yourself up before you move off
sections.body:
Adjust everything while the car is still standing still. Fiddling with a mirror halfway onto Frankfurter Allee is exactly how cyclists get hurt.

**Seat.** Bottom and back firmly into the seat, close enough that you can press the clutch and brake fully with the **knee still slightly bent**. Backrest fairly upright: a reclined seat looks relaxed and lets you slide under the belt in a crash.

**Steering wheel.** With your shoulders touching the backrest, your wrists should just reach the top of the rim. That leaves your arms **slightly bent** at the 9-and-3 grip, so you can turn quickly and the airbag has room to do its job. Straight, locked arms are the classic beginner's error.

**Head restraint (Kopfstütze).** A crash device, not a pillow. Its **top edge belongs roughly level with the top of your head**, with only a small gap to the back of your head. Set too low, it becomes a pivot for your neck in a rear-end shunt, precisely the whiplash it exists to prevent.

**Mirrors.** Interior mirror plus both door mirrors, each showing a narrow strip of your own car so you have a reference for judging distance. Then accept the truth: a blind spot (*toter Winkel*) survives even perfect adjustment. Before pulling out, changing lanes, or turning right across a Berlin cycle lane, you also look **over your shoulder**.

callout.text: Order of operations: seat, backrest, head restraint, wheel, mirrors, belt. Move the seat afterwards and the mirrors are wrong again.

sections.heading: Belts and small passengers
sections.body:
Prescribed seatbelts **must be worn while driving**: every seat, every trip, including the 600 m to the Späti. Not wearing one costs 30 €, and every adult answers for their own buckle. Wear it properly: the shoulder strap over the **middle of the shoulder** (never across the neck), the lap strap **low across the hips** (not over the belly), no twists, no thick padded coat underneath adding slack, and never tucked behind your back to silence the buzzer.

The law grants only a few narrow exceptions: driving at **walking pace**, such as reversing or shuffling around a car park; **door-to-door delivery** work where you keep getting out within your delivery district; and passengers in buses where standing is permitted. Taxi drivers are *not* exempt, and that myth died decades ago. (An individual exemption, for instance on medical grounds, has to be granted by the authorities; you cannot award it to yourself.)

**Children.** A child needs an approved, suitable child restraint (*Kinderrückhalteeinrichtung*) if it is **under 12 years old AND shorter than 150 cm**. Both conditions must apply, so the duty ends as soon as *either* falls away: the 12th birthday, or 150 cm of height. A tall ten-year-old of 1.55 m may legally use the normal belt; a small thirteen-year-old may too. Carrying a child with **no restraint at all** costs the driver 60 € **and a point in Flensburg** (70 € and a point if several children are unsecured); using an unsuitable or badly fitted restraint is a 30 € warning fine, 35 € for several children.

**The airbag trap.** A rear-facing seat (*Reboarder*, baby carrier) on the front passenger seat is only permissible if the **front passenger airbag is deactivated**, by key switch or at a dealer. An inflating airbag strikes the back of the shell with enormous force, straight into the child's head, and sliding the seat back does not help. Switch the airbag on again the moment the child seat comes out. The rear seat is always the better answer.

callout.text: Rear-facing child seat + live front airbag = forbidden and potentially fatal. Airbag off, or child in the back.

sections.heading: Loading: physics does not care about your IKEA run
sections.body:
**Rule one.** The load, the lashing gear and any load-carrying equipment must be stowed and secured so that nothing can **slide, tip over, roll about, fall off or make avoidable noise, even under emergency braking or a sudden swerve**. A shut tailgate is not "secured". At 50 km/h a loose toolbox arrives at the back of your head with the force of a small motorbike.

Practical version: heavy items **low down and pushed forward** against the rear seat backs, lighter things on top, gaps filled, lashing straps and an anti-slip mat rather than optimism. Nothing loose on the parcel shelf. And the load must never hide your **number plate or your lights**. A bike rack on the towbar needs its own repeat plate and lighting board.

**Sticking out.** Vehicle plus load may be at most **2.55 m wide and 4 m high**. To the rear the load may project up to **1.5 m**, and up to **3 m** on a journey of no more than 100 km. To the front nothing may project at all below a height of 2.50 m; above that, 50 cm at most. If the load projects **more than 1 m beyond the car's rear reflectors**, mark it: a bright red flag of at least **30 × 30 cm** held open by a crossbar, or an equally large red board hung so it swings across the direction of travel, or a red cylinder of the same size, mounted no higher than 1.50 m above the road. In darkness add a red light there, plus a red reflector no higher than 90 cm. Sideways, a load reaching more than 40 cm past the outer edge of your position or tail lamps must be marked whenever lighting is needed, with a white light to the front and a red one to the rear, no higher than 1.50 m above the road.

**Weights.** The **permissible gross mass** (*zulässige Gesamtmasse*) is printed in your registration document (*Zulassungsbescheinigung Teil I*); your **payload** (*Zuladung*) is that figure minus the car's empty mass, and passengers count. **Roof load** (*Dachlast*) is a separate limit set by the manufacturer, typically 50–100 kg on a car, and the **rack and empty box count towards it**. Weight up there also lifts the centre of gravity, so ease off in bends and expect the car to squirm in crosswinds.

Overloading is not a paperwork sin. Braking distances stretch, tyres run beyond their rated load and can overheat and burst, the suspension bottoms out and the steering answers late and lazily. It is an offence for the driver and for the registered keeper (*Halter*), and if it contributed to a crash, expect that to feature in the blame.

callout.text: Rear overhang cheat sheet: up to 1.5 m normally, up to 3 m only for trips of 100 km or less, and anything more than 1 m past the rear reflectors gets the red 30 × 30 cm flag.

sections.heading: Trailers, towing and driving green
sections.body:
**What class B tows.** As far as the licence is concerned: a trailer with a permissible gross mass of up to **750 kg**. Something heavier only if the **whole combination** stays within **3,500 kg** permissible gross mass. (Your car's own towing limits in the papers still apply on top of that.) Need more? **B96** is a short course at a driving school covering theory, manoeuvring and a drive, with **no exam**, and it lifts the combination to **4,250 kg**. Full class **BE** requires a practical test and allows a trailer of up to **3,500 kg**.

Speed with a trailer: **80 km/h** outside built-up areas, Autobahn included. With a Tempo-100 approval and its technical conditions met (stabiliser or suitable shock absorbers, tyres in good condition, certificate on board) you may do 100 km/h on Autobahnen and Kraftfahrstraßen.

**Nose weight (Stützlast).** That is the downward force the trailer's drawbar puts on the tow ball. Stay within the **lowest** of the three figures for car, towbar and trailer, and remember it presses on the rear axle, so it counts against the **car's** payload. Too *little* nose weight is dangerous in its own right: a tail-heavy trailer starts to snake at speed. So load heavy items over the trailer's axle, use as much of the permitted nose weight as you can, and clip on the breakaway cable.

**Towing a breakdown (Abschleppen).** Both vehicles switch on their **hazard warning lights**. **Motorcycles may not be towed at all.** If the car died **on the Autobahn**, you must **leave it at the next exit**, and if it broke down elsewhere, you may not join the Autobahn to tow it. Towing is for getting a casualty out of traffic and as far as the nearest garage, not a free ride home. The person being towed needs a licence, the ignition on (or the steering locks), and gentle brake work to keep the rope taut.

**Eco-driving (spritsparende Fahrweise).** The exam loves this and so does your wallet: shift up **early**, around 2,000 rpm, skip gears, and cruise in the highest gear that still pulls smoothly. Read the traffic far ahead and lift off instead of braking, because a modern engine on overrun injects no fuel at all. Switch the engine **off** whenever you will be waiting a while: a closed level crossing, a jam at a standstill, a long red light. Letting a parked engine "warm up" wastes fuel and is exactly the unnecessary noise and exhaust the StVO forbids. Correct tyre pressure, no roof box you are not using, no dead weight in the boot, moderate air conditioning.

**Berlin's Umweltzone.** The whole area inside the S-Bahn ring is a low-emission zone (sign 270.1). Your car needs the **green emissions sticker** (*grüne Feinstaubplakette*) on the windscreen; driving in without one costs **100 €**, and a valid HU sticker is no substitute.

callout.text: Class B trailer maths: 750 kg always; heavier only if car + trailer stay within 3.5 t. B96 = 4.25 t combination (training, no test). BE = trailer up to 3.5 t (test).

key_takeaways: 1.6 mm is the legal tread minimum, but change summer tyres at about 3 mm and winter tyres at about 4 mm.
Winter duty is situational, not calendar-based: wintry road, then all four wheels with the Alpine symbol.
Every prescribed light must work, day and night; a red warning lamp means stop now, not later.
Head restraint level with the top of your head, knee slightly bent, arms slightly bent, then mirrors.
Child seat while under 12 AND under 150 cm; rear-facing seat in front only with the airbag switched off.
Secure every load against a full emergency stop, and mark anything more than 1 m past the rear reflectors with a red 30 × 30 cm flag.
Class B: 750 kg trailer, or heavier only within a 3,500 kg combination; B96 = 4,250 kg, BE = 3,500 kg trailer.
Towing: hazard lights on both cars, motorcycles never, and off the Autobahn at the next exit.

german_terms.en: Alpine symbol: three-peaked mountain with a snowflake, the winter tyre marking
nose weight on the tow ball

questions.text: How deep must the main tread grooves of a car tyre be at the very least, all the way around the tyre? Answer in millimetres.
questions.explanation: The StVZO requires a tread depth of at least 1.6 mm in the main tread grooves, around the whole circumference of the tyre. Below that the tyre is illegal: 60 € and a point in Flensburg, and after a crash your insurer will look at it very closely. Treat 1.6 mm as the point where a tyre is already dangerous rather than as a target, because wet grip and aquaplaning resistance fall away well before you get there, which is why testers recommend changing summer tyres at about 3 mm and winter tyres at about 4 mm.

questions.text: How should you look after your tyres between garage visits?

options.text: Check the pressures regularly, roughly every two weeks and before a long trip, on cold tyres, using the car maker's values.
Running slightly less pressure than specified is on the safe side, because a softer tyre grips better.
A tyre's age is irrelevant as long as there is still enough tread on it.

questions.explanation: The maker's pressures are on a sticker in the fuel filler flap or on the driver's door pillar, and they change with the load. Measure cold, because a warm tyre reads higher. Running soft is not "gentler": the tyre flexes and overheats and can fail at speed, the shoulders wear away, and the steering goes vague and you burn more fuel. Too much pressure is no better, because the middle of the tread wears and the contact patch shrinks. Age matters too, because rubber hardens over the years and grips worse even with plenty of tread, so a pressure check is a good moment to look at the DOT date and for cracks.

questions.text: It has snowed overnight and the road through Prenzlauer Berg is covered in slush. Which statements are correct?

options.text: You may only drive if all wheels are fitted with tyres carrying the Alpine symbol (a three-peaked mountain with a snowflake).
Since 1 October 2024 the old "M+S" marking on its own is no longer sufficient.
The winter tyre duty applies by the calendar, from 1 November until Easter, whatever the weather does.

questions.explanation: Germany has no calendar rule. The duty is triggered by the road, not the date. Whenever there is Glatteis, Schneeglätte, Schneematsch, Eisglätte or Reifglätte, every wheel (not just the driven axle) must have tyres meeting StVZO §36 (4), and since 1 October 2024 that means the Alpine symbol; the transitional period for older M+S tyres ended on 30 September 2024. So an M+S or all-season tyre without the little mountain is legally a summer tyre now. Driving on the wrong tyres in wintry conditions costs 60 € and a point, more if you obstruct or endanger others. "Von O bis O" (October to Easter) is a good habit, not the law.

questions.text: What can you tell from a tyre's sidewall and its tread?

options.text: The four DOT digits give the week and year of manufacture, so "0824" means week 8 of 2024.
A tyre worn down to 1.6 mm grips just as well on a wet road as one with 4 mm of tread.
German law requires car tyres to be replaced once they are four years old.

questions.explanation: The DOT code's last four digits are the production date: week, then year. There is no legal age limit for car tyres, but the rubber hardens over the years, so most experts suggest replacing them after roughly six to eight years even with tread left, and treat a hard, cracked old tyre as suspect regardless. On depth, remember that 1.6 mm is the legal floor, not a safe level: with less than about 3 mm the grooves can no longer clear water fast enough and aquaplaning starts at much lower speeds.

questions.text: How do you keep on top of your vehicle's lighting?

options.text: Walk round the car from time to time with the lights switched on. A bulb can fail without you noticing anything.
You can check your brake lights alone by reversing slowly towards a shop window or garage door and watching the reflection as you press the pedal.
If one dipped-beam headlight has failed you may carry on for now, because one working headlight is enough.

questions.explanation: The prescribed lighting must be fitted, working and ready for use, in daylight too, so a blown bulb is already a defect you are responsible for, and a car with one headlight is easily mistaken for a motorbike at night. Brake lights and indicators are the ones you cannot see from your seat, hence the reflection trick or a helper standing behind the car. Carrying spare bulbs and a look at the lenses (dirty glass costs you a lot of light) belong to the same habit.

questions.text: A red warning lamp lights up on your dashboard while you are driving. What is correct?

options.text: If it is the oil-pressure lamp, stop as soon as you safely can and switch the engine off.
If it is the brake warning lamp, stop and have the brakes checked instead of driving on.
Red lamps are only reminders, so you can finish your journey and see a garage next week.

questions.explanation: The colour is the message: red means act immediately, yellow means have it looked at soon. Driving on with no oil pressure can destroy an engine within minutes, and a seizing engine in the middle of the Stadtring is a safety problem, not just a repair bill. A brake warning lamp points to low brake fluid or a fault in the braking system, so the one component you cannot do without may fail exactly when you need it. Coolant temperature and the charge lamp are red for the same reason. Get off the road, hazard lights on, warning triangle out, and call for help rather than gambling on the last few kilometres.

questions.text: You are setting up the driver's seat in an unfamiliar car. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Set the seat so that your knee is still slightly bent when a pedal is pressed all the way down.
Adjust the head restraint so that its top edge is roughly level with the top of your head.
Sit close enough that your arms stay slightly bent when you hold the wheel at 9 and 3.

questions.explanation: You need reserve travel in your legs to brake with full force, and bent arms to turn the wheel quickly and to let the airbag deploy into your chest rather than into straightened, locked elbows, so "far back with straight arms" is the classic beginner's mistake. A good check: with your shoulders against the backrest, your wrists should just reach the top of the rim. The head restraint is crash equipment, not a cushion. Set too low it becomes a pivot for your neck in a rear-end shunt and causes the whiplash it should prevent. Do all of this while parked, then the mirrors, then the belt.

questions.text: What does the law say about seatbelts?

options.text: The shoulder strap must lie over the middle of the shoulder and the lap strap low across the hips, with no twists.
The belt duty does not apply when driving at walking pace, for example when reversing or manoeuvring on a car park.
Taxi drivers are exempt from wearing a belt while they are carrying passengers.

questions.explanation: Prescribed belts must be worn while driving, and not wearing one costs 30 €. The exceptions are deliberately narrow: walking-pace manoeuvring, door-to-door delivery work with constant stops inside the delivery district, and passengers in buses where standing is allowed. The old taxi exemption is long gone. Fit matters as much as the law: over the neck or over a padded coat the belt cannot hold your pelvis and chest, and a belt run under the arm or behind the back is worse than useless in a crash.

questions.text: When must a child travel in an approved child restraint (child seat)?

options.text: While the child is under 12 years old and shorter than 150 cm.
An 11-year-old who is 1.55 m tall may legally use the normal seat belt.
Height is irrelevant: every child under 12 must sit in a child seat.

questions.explanation: Both conditions have to be true at the same time, so the duty ends as soon as either one falls away: the 12th birthday or 150 cm of height. The restraint must be officially approved and suitable for that child's size and weight; a booster that is too big leaves the lap belt across the abdomen instead of the hips. The driver is responsible, not the passenger in the back: a child carried with no restraint at all costs 60 € and a point in Flensburg, 70 € and a point if several are unsecured, while a wrong or badly fitted seat is a 30 € warning fine. Even once a child is legally out of a seat, the back is the safer place.

questions.text: A friend asks you to carry her baby in a rear-facing baby carrier on the front passenger seat. What applies?

options.text: A rear-facing child seat must not be used on a front passenger seat with an active front airbag.
It is fine as long as you slide the passenger seat all the way back.
It is permitted without further precautions because a baby carrier is always fitted facing backwards.

questions.explanation: A front airbag inflates within milliseconds with enormous force, and in a rear-facing seat the back of the shell, and therefore the baby's head, sits right in its path. That is why every child seat manual and the warning label on the sun visor forbid the combination, and sliding the seat back does not create nearly enough space. If the child really must travel in front facing backwards, the passenger airbag has to be deactivated first (key switch or dealer) and switched on again the moment the seat comes out. Far better: put the child in the back, which is the safest place in the car anyway.

questions.text: You are driving a friend's flat-pack furniture home in an estate car. How must the load be dealt with?

options.text: It must be stowed and secured so that nothing can slide, tip over, roll about or fall off even under emergency braking or a sudden swerve.
Heavy items belong low down and pushed forward against the rear seat backs.
Loose boxes stacked above the level of the seat backs are acceptable on a short trip.

questions.explanation: The StVO sets the standard at full emergency braking and an evasive swerve, not at gentle driving, because that is when loads actually move. In a 50 km/h impact an unsecured object keeps flying at 50 km/h until something stops it, often the back of your head, which is why nothing should be piled above the seat backs. Use lashing straps and an anti-slip mat, fill the gaps, keep heavy things low and forward so the car's handling stays predictable, and never let the load block your view, your lights or your number plate.

questions.text: You are collecting long planks and driving less than 100 km with them. How far may the load project beyond the rear of your car at most? Answer in metres.
questions.explanation: The normal limit for a rear overhang is 1.5 m, but for journeys of no more than 100 km the law allows up to 3 m. That is the limit for the total projection, not a licence to skip the safety kit: anything sticking out more than 1 m past the car's rear reflectors must be marked with a bright red flag, board or cylinder of at least 30 × 30 cm, no higher than 1.50 m above the road, plus a red light and a red reflector in the dark. And bear in mind what a long overhang does to your driving: it swings out wide over the pavement whenever you turn.

questions.text: A ladder projects a long way out of the back of your car. What is correct about marking it?

options.text: It has to be marked if it projects more than 1 m beyond the car's rear reflectors.
A bright red flag, a hanging board or a cylinder of at least 30 × 30 cm can be used as the marking.
In darkness the end of the load is marked with a white light.

questions.explanation: The reference point is the rear reflectors, not the bumper, and the marking device must be bright red and at least 30 × 30 cm: a flag held open by a crossbar, an equally large board hung so it swings across the direction of travel, or a red cylinder of the same size, mounted no higher than 1.50 m above the road so following drivers actually see it. At night, or whenever visibility requires it, you additionally need a red light at the end of the load and a red reflector no more than 90 cm above the road. White to the rear is wrong in principle: white shows the front of a vehicle, red the back.

questions.text: You have fitted roof bars and a rear bike rack for a weekend trip. Which statements are correct?

options.text: A roof load raises the centre of gravity, so take bends more gently and expect the car to react more to crosswinds.
The weight of the roof bars and the empty box counts towards the permitted roof load.
A rear bike rack may cover the number plate and the rear lights as long as the bikes themselves are strapped down properly.

questions.explanation: The permitted roof load (Dachlast) is set by the manufacturer, often only 50 to 100 kg, and it covers everything up there, carrier and box included, so the usable payload is smaller than people assume. Weight high up makes the car roll more in bends and more nervous in gusts, and it costs a surprising amount of fuel, so take the rack off when the trip is over. Number plate and lights must always stay visible and effective: if the rack hides them, you need a repeat plate and a lighting board on the rack.

questions.text: Your registration document shows a permissible gross mass of 1,850 kg and an empty mass of 1,420 kg. How much may you still load in total (people plus luggage)? Answer in kilograms.
questions.explanation: Payload = permissible gross mass minus empty mass, so 1,850 kg − 1,420 kg = 430 kg. The catch is that passengers count: four adults and their bags will eat most of 430 kg before you have even loaded the boot, and a roof box plus bars comes off the same budget. Both figures are in the Zulassungsbescheinigung Teil I. Exceeding them is not a formality: braking distances grow, the tyres run beyond their rated load, and both the driver and the registered keeper can be fined.

questions.text: Why does overloading a car matter so much?

options.text: The braking distance gets longer and the car reacts less precisely to the steering.
Overloaded tyres can overheat and burst.
Because the car is heavier it presses onto the road harder, so it actually brakes better.

questions.explanation: Brakes, tyres, springs and dampers are all designed for the permissible masses in the papers. Beyond them the brakes have more energy to dissipate and fade sooner, and the tyres flex and heat up past what their load index allows, the suspension bottoms out, and the car rolls and wanders where it used to feel planted. The idea that extra weight improves braking is a classic exam trap: more mass means more kinetic energy to get rid of, so the stopping distance grows. Also watch the axle loads. A boot packed to the roof can overload the rear axle even when the total mass is still legal.

questions.text: What may you tow with an ordinary class B licence?

options.text: A trailer with a permissible gross mass of up to 750 kg.
A heavier trailer, provided the permissible gross mass of the whole combination does not exceed 3,500 kg.
Any combination up to a permissible gross mass of 4,250 kg.

questions.explanation: Class B covers vehicles up to 3,500 kg permissible gross mass, plus a trailer of up to 750 kg. Above 750 kg the trailer is still allowed as long as car and trailer together stay within 3,500 kg, so a 1,900 kg car leaves room for a 1,600 kg trailer on paper. The 4,250 kg figure belongs to the B96 key number, not to plain B. Remember that the licence is only half the story: your car's own permitted towing weight, nose weight and axle loads still apply, and they are usually the tighter limit.

questions.text: You want to tow something heavier. Which statements are correct?

options.text: The B96 key number is obtained through driving-school training without an examination and allows combinations of more than 3,500 kg up to 4,250 kg.
Class BE allows a trailer with a permissible gross mass of up to 3,500 kg.
The less nose weight (Stützlast) there is on the tow ball, the more stable the trailer runs.

questions.explanation: B96 is a short course of theory, manoeuvring practice and a drive, with a certificate at the end and no test;  it is entered in your licence and stretches the combination to 4,250 kg. Class BE needs a practical examination and then permits a trailer of up to 3,500 kg behind a class B vehicle. Nose weight works the other way round from the third option: a trailer loaded tail-heavy, with too little weight on the ball, starts to snake at speed. Load heavy items over the trailer's axle, use as much of the permitted nose weight as you can, and remember that it presses on your car's rear axle and counts against its payload.

questions.text: A friend's car has broken down and you are going to tow it with a rope. What applies?

options.text: Both vehicles must have their hazard warning lights switched on while towing.
If the car broke down on the Autobahn, you must leave the Autobahn at the next exit.
A broken-down motorcycle may be towed by rope as far as the next garage.

questions.explanation: Towing is an emergency measure to get a casualty out of the traffic flow, so both vehicles run their hazard warning lights, and a vehicle recovered on the Autobahn has to leave it at the next exit. You may not simply carry on towing down the motorway, and if the breakdown happened elsewhere you may not enter the Autobahn to tow it at all. Motorcycles must never be towed: with no stabilising rider input at the rope they are impossible to control. Practical points for the person being towed: licence required, ignition on so the steering does not lock, and gentle braking to keep the rope taut. With the engine dead, steering and brakes need far more force.

questions.text: You want to drive more cheaply and more cleanly through Berlin. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Shifting up early and driving in the highest gear that still pulls smoothly saves fuel.
If you know you will be waiting a while, at a closed level crossing or in a jam at a standstill, switch the engine off.
You may drive into Berlin's Umweltzone without the green emissions sticker as long as your car has a valid HU.

questions.explanation: Low revs in a high gear, gentle throttle and anticipation are where the savings are: look far ahead, lift off early and let the car roll, because a modern engine injects no fuel at all on the overrun, and every avoided braking manoeuvre is fuel you did not burn. An idling engine does zero km per litre, so switch it off for longer waits and never warm it up while parked. That is exactly the unnecessary exhaust and noise the StVO forbids. Correct tyre pressures, no unused roof box and less dead weight help too. And the sticker is a separate matter entirely: the whole area inside the S-Bahn ring is a low-emission zone, entering it without a valid green Feinstaubplakette costs 100 €, and the roadworthiness test has nothing to do with it.
